Lessons.Title: Reasoning about Angles (Part 1)
ExplanationParagraphs:
Learning goal: You will the purpose of this lesson is twofold: for you to use known angles to reason about unknown angles on a clock, and for them to practice drawing angles of given measurements.
Angles are ever present on an analog clock. In this lesson, you investigate and solve problems about the angles formed by a clock’s hour and minute hands. You reason about the number of degrees between the two hands or the number of degrees the minute hand has turned over some specified time.

2021 lesson activities: Warm-up: Which One Doesn’t Belong: Time After Time (10 minutes); Activity 1: Draw a Clock (15 minutes); Activity 2: Tick Tock (20 minutes); Cool-down: One Angle at a Time (5 minutes)
Corrected mathematical focus: Use a clock as a 360° circle with 12 equal 30° sectors; construct angles from known positions and turns.

Edulytics authored guidance: Draw perpendicular vertical and horizontal diameters to locate 12, 3, 6 and 9. Divide each quadrant into three equal 30° clock sectors. At exactly 4:00, four sectors between 12 and 4 produce a 120° smaller angle.
First-party Cool-down (not publisher assessment): What is the smaller angle at exactly 4:00? Show clock-sector reasoning.
Images, drawing/protractor accuracy, partner tasks and the gated original publisher Cool-down require original task evidence and teacher/visual review.

Original 2021 source source-verified locally in earlier Our-CS intake: Which One Doesn't Belong: Time After Time uses four illustrated clocks, not interchangeable exact-hour pictures; teacher checks actual hand positions. Draw a Clock asks learners to use intersecting perpendicular lines to place 12, 3, 6, 9 at 90° intervals and subdivide the clock's 12 hours into 30° sectors. Tick Tock asks angles at 6:00 (180°) and 8:00 (smaller angle 120°); other source clock images need visual inspection.

Digital REUSE: previous exact-hour comparison family is supplementary for exact times on the hour with minute hand at 12. It does NOT calculate arbitrary partial-minute source pictures; class-drawn clocks and their rays are teacher-checked.

WorkedExamples.Title: Clock 12 equal spaces, source activity
WorkedExamples.Question: A student draws perpendicular diameters on a clock. What angular spacing separates consecutive numbers?
WorkedExamples.Method: Full turn 360° divided into 12 equal sectors.
Steps: 12 to 8 spans 4 smaller gaps counterclockwise, 120 degrees.
WorkedExamples.Check: Exact-hour benchmark math, not arbitrary time extrapolation.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Treating figures as only their appearance.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Ignores the necessary mathematical attributes or turn sizes.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Use a clock as a 360° circle with 12 equal 30° sectors; construct angles from known positions and turns.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Assuming a drawing, classification or calculation is correct from appearance alone.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The original task requires a mathematical attribute or reasoning check.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Use the original constraints and this rule: Use a clock as a 360° circle with 12 equal 30° sectors; construct angles from known positions and turns.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Treating an arbitrary clock graphic as an exact-hour case.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The warm-up clocks include hand positions between marks and require observing their original images.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Only use exact-hour numeric generator when minute hand is precisely on 12 and hour hand on a numbered mark.
